setup: The Eurasian steppe is a belt of open grassland running almost unbroken from the Black Sea to Manchuria — too dry to farm, perfect for grazing. A people who could turn that grass into horses and mounted archers could field armies no settled kingdom could catch, but grass is not silk, iron, or grain, so every steppe power lived by some answer to one problem: how a grass economy gets the products of a grain economy, above all from China. At the heart of it sat the Orkhon valley in what is now Mongolia, the steppe's throne room, where whoever ruled was held to hold the legitimate center of nomadic power. In the 740s that throne belonged to the Türks — the Ashina clan who had given the world the very word Turk — but their Second Khaganate was brittle and resented by its subject tribes. The largest block of those subjects, a Turkic people called the Uyghurs, was about to take everything: the throne, the capital region, and very nearly the name.

bridge: Chapter 1 left a Turkic people who were not the Türks holding the Orkhon, the steppe's throne. The Uyghurs had overthrown the old Ashina dynasty, planted a walled capital at Ordu-Baliq, organized power through the Nine Tribes, and announced themselves to China by couriering the last Türk emperor's head to the Tang court. Their qaghan Bayanchur had turned a victorious tribal coalition into an actual state with a city and an alphabet's worth of writing. But none of that explained how a grass empire got rich enough to pay for stone cities — that money did not come from the grass. It came from a disaster about to erupt downriver, in the heart of Tang China.
setup: For most of recorded history the steppe wanted what China had, and China paid the nomads to go away. The Uyghurs inverted it. In 755 Tang China was arguably the wealthiest, most populous empire in the world, its capital Chang'an holding perhaps a million people. Then one of its own border generals, the half-Sogdian half-Türk commander An Lushan, revolted with a battle-hardened frontier army and inside six months took both Tang capitals. The dynasty did not fall, but it came within reach of it, and a court in that condition needed cavalry it did not have — immediately. It looked north, to the new power on the Orkhon. What is at stake here is the strangest creditor relationship in premodern history: for about a decade China did not pay the steppe to stay away, but begged it to come in, and then could not afford to make it leave.

bridge: Chapters 1 and 2 built a steppe empire that broke every rule: a walled capital on the Orkhon, written records in the Uyghurs' own voice, and — after the An Lushan rebellion — a structural grip on Tang China through the horse-and-silk trade, in which broken-winded steppe horses were swapped for new silk at a rate the humiliated Tang could not refuse. Silk was currency across Inner Asia, so the Uyghurs had built a pipeline taxing a grain economy on a permanent schedule, run for them by the Sogdian merchants of Samarkand and Bukhara who were already the court's scribes and financiers. The Uyghurs had solved the material half of the steppe's old problem. This chapter is about the cultural half — and the single most unusual decision in the entire history of the steppe.
setup: Steppe religion was normally Tengrism: a sky-centered system named for Tengri the sky god, with no scripture, no founder, no missionary clergy, and no church — the kind of faith a mobile, pre-literate people carries in its head. What the Uyghurs adopted was its near-opposite. Manichaeism was a bookish dualist religion founded by the prophet Mani in third-century Sasanian Persia, teaching a cosmic war between Light and Darkness and demanding strict asceticism. Designed for export, persecuted nearly out of Persia, it survived along the Silk Road financed by those same Sogdian merchants. In 762–763 the qaghan Bögü Khan, occupying a Luoyang his cavalry was sacking, met Sogdian Manichaean clergy and took them home — and made an ascetic, vegetarian, animal-sparing faith the state religion of an empire whose entire economy was animals. Why a horse-emperor did this is the kind of question this book weighs rather than settles.

bridge: By the start of the ninth century the Uyghurs had built something no steppe empire had built before: an urban, literate, mercantile state on the Orkhon, tied by religion and credit to the Sogdian networks and by arms and trade to China. Bögü Khan's Manichaean court ran the only foreign scriptural church the steppe ever sponsored, and the Old Uyghur script gave it an administrative literacy. But the empire that looked the most settled-looking nomad power yet had quietly traded the nomad's classic invulnerability for a settled state's classic fragilities — it lived off a single trade relationship, defended one fixed capital, leaned on a foreign merchant diaspora, and had no deep agrarian base of its own to fall back on. In the 830s the trade, the herds, and the weather all failed at once.
setup: Steppe empires usually die slowly — a confederation frays, tribes drift to a rival over a decade. The Uyghur Khaganate did not. From the 820s the throne stopped being able to deliver the two things that held the Nine Tribes together, military success and a cut of the China trade, as a run of qaghans were enthroned and then murdered by their own ministers, burning legitimacy a tribal confederation cannot easily regrow. Then a catastrophic winter at the end of the 830s — a jut, when ice seals the grass and the herds starve standing in it — brought epidemic and famine the fixed-capital empire could not absorb. A disaffected general guided the Yenisei Kyrgyz, longstanding Uyghur enemies to the north, down onto the weakened heartland. The walled city Bayanchur had built to display permanence was about to become the very thing that made the dynasty mortal: an address whose burning could be the death of the state.

bridge: In 840 the Yenisei Kyrgyz stormed and burned Ordu-Baliq, killed the qaghan, and ended the Uyghur Khaganate in a single campaigning season — then looted the Orkhon and withdrew to Siberia rather than rule it, leaving the steppe's throne empty. The surviving Uyghurs broke into three migrations: one south to the old Tang creditor, broken at the Battle of Shahu in 843; one west into the Gansu corridor; and one southwest into the oasis towns of the Tarim Basin, the great desert ring of Silk Road cities in what is now Xinjiang. The empire was gone; the people, their literacy, and their commercial habits were not. This chapter is the strangest second act in steppe history.
setup: The usual fate of a shattered steppe people is absorption — taken in by whoever beat them, intermarried, gone within two generations. The Uyghurs did the opposite: they kept their identity, their script, and their elite culture by deliberately ceasing to be nomads. Around 866 a Uyghur leader took the Turfan oases and founded the Kingdom of Qocho, which lasted roughly five centuries, far longer than the khaganate that spawned it. Moving into deeply Buddhist oasis towns, and no longer needing the Sogdian-Manichaean trade reason to stay Manichaean, the descendants of Bögü Khan's court drifted to Buddhism — patronage following popular practice rather than leading it. They became farmers, blooming one of the hottest, driest places in Asia with the karez underground canals, and they kept their literacy and their merchant instincts. The payoff is not the flourishing. It is what a settled, literate, administratively skilled people becomes worth to the conqueror who comes next.

bridge: Chapter 5 followed the Uyghurs east, into the Buddhist oasis kingdom of Qocho, where a destroyed nomad empire reinvented itself as a settled, literate, farming civilization that would one day staff the Mongol chancery. Now the book doubles back to a thread planted and left hanging in Chapter 1: the Karluks, the third partner in the 742 revolt against the Türks, who took the western steppe — the Ili and Chu valleys around Lake Balkhash — while the Uyghurs took the center. For a century the Karluks are a name in the margin. In the tenth century they and the confederation they led do something that reshapes a third of the world's religious map.
setup: Before Islam the Karluks were what the eastern Uyghurs had been before the oases: a pastoral, Tengri-worshipping steppe power. What made them pivotal was their address. The confederation they formed, the Kara-Khanid Khanate, ruled from Kashgar and Balasagun and sat directly on the frontier of the Samanids, the brilliant Persian Islamic dynasty ruling Transoxiana and Khurasan from Bukhara — whose cities, scholars, and Sufi preachers the Kara-Khanid Turks raided, traded with, and increasingly lived alongside. They were the last great pagan Turkic power on the doorstep of the settled Islamic world. Around 934, by a tradition the sources tell in pious hindsight, a prince named Satuq Bughra Khan converted and seized power from his pagan uncle, and made Islam the religion of his line. Individual Turks had been Muslim for two centuries as slave soldiers and merchants; the distinction here, the one this chapter turns on, is that the Kara-Khanids were the first Turkic Muslim state — a dynasty ruling Turkic people on the steppe making Islam its own.

bridge: The book has now followed two opposite afterlives from one Uyghur-Turkic steppe world. East, at Qocho, the Uyghurs became a Buddhist, literate, agrarian people (Chapter 5). West, the Karluk-led Kara-Khanids became the first Turkic Muslim state, took Bukhara and ended the Samanids in 999, and gave Islam its first Turkic literature before the Seljuks absorbed them (Chapter 6). Both halves of that world were proud, intact, and Muslim or Buddhist on their own terms. In the twelfth century both were swallowed by the same improbable third party — not a Muslim power and not a steppe pagan one, but a Buddhist Chinese-style dynasty in flight from the far side of Asia.
setup: The premise of this chapter sounds invented, and every clause of it is attested. In 1125 the Jurchen destroyed the Liao dynasty of the Khitan, a Mongolic horse-people who had ruled north China for two centuries. Out of the wreck a Liao imperial prince, Yelü Dashi — who held the jinshi, the highest Chinese civil-service degree — led a few thousand followers two thousand miles west, gathered tribes, absorbed the old Uyghur and Kara-Khanid lands, and around 1132 proclaimed himself Gurkhan, founding the Qara-Khitai. In 1141 at the Battle of Qatwan near Samarkand he annihilated the army of Ahmad Sanjar, the most powerful Muslim ruler in the east — the largest defeat of a Muslim army in Central Asia to that point. What this Buddhist dynasty then did with Muslim Central Asia inverts every expectation the rest of the book has set up, and its fragility is the structural lesson the book keeps returning to.

bridge: Chapter 7 left the Qara-Khitai — the Buddhist, Chinese-institutioned dynasty that ruled Muslim Central Asia by tolerant indirect rule and famously light taxation — overstretched and brittle. The system worked only while the center could still win, and by the 1190s the Khwarazm-Shahs in the southwest were strong enough to stop paying. The whole half-millennium this book has followed — Uyghur khaganate, Buddhist oases, Muslim Kara-Khanids, Buddhist Qara-Khitai — was now one hard shock from the end. The shock arrived from the east, in the person of a defeated prince fleeing a man the next several stories in this project are about.
setup: Every story in this project ends by handing the reader to what comes next; this one hands the reader to the Mongol Empire. Far to the east, on the Mongolian steppe the Uyghurs had abandoned in 840 and no one had ruled since, a war-leader named Temüjin spent two decades destroying his rivals, and in 1206 an assembly proclaimed him Genghis Khan — putting an emperor back on the Orkhon after 366 empty years. The forgotten half-millennium does not simply get conquered. Its three converging endings between 1204 and 1218 — the Buddhist Uyghur idiqut of Qocho submitting voluntarily and early, the fugitive Naiman prince Küchlüg usurping the Qara-Khitai and wrecking its tolerance, and the Mongol general Jebe taking the realm by restoring that tolerance — fold this world into the machinery of the Mongol conquest. The pen the Mongols conquered with, it turns out, was cut on the Orkhon.
